utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Witness, before we take a break, two matters. First, I invited you to write down names and names of companies of those who stayed within those companies. Have you done so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't write that. I cannot remember the exact names. Juso, Yugo, Split, that is for customs duty on goods. Now, there's this one in the municipality I cannot remember. There was this Muslim from Kotor Varos who was in my secretariat. He was a lot older than I am, but I simply cannot remember his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you remember names, please write them down. If you don't remember names, of course you cannot write them down. That's clear. That's one. Second, you may remember that before the last break we had some questions about the decision of the 22nd of June, 1992, to be implemented by the 26th of June, where you said that you were not relieved from your duties, although you did not implement that order, and then we later established that you had stayed in your position until the 15th of June. Now, just to clarify matters, when you said you stayed until the 15th of June, I assumed - but please correct me when I'm wrong - that you were referring to the 15th of June, 1992. Is that -- was that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, 15th of June. 15th of June, 1992. But I remained in this function of the secretariat and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. Then we well understood that you were referring to 1992. You may follow the usher. And we'll take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom, I would like to briefly stay attention to Exhibit D314. On the 14th of October of this year, the Defence indicated that it wished to withdraw Exhibit D314 as it was satisfied with the content of Exhibit P1640 in evidence. The Chamber accepts this withdrawal and hereby instructs the Registry to mark D314 as not admitted in e-court and to include in the additional comments column a note that D314 was withdrawn in light of P1640.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P2900, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a report from a Banja Luka CSB commission from August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have page 10 of the English and 13 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I didn't see the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, we're looking here at a portion of the report related to Bosanski Novi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we should follow the instructions of Mr. Traldi rather than spontaneously respond to what the witness said. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page in the B/C/S and in the middle of the page in the English, we read: "Pursuant to the decision on the voluntary resettlement of citizens of the government of the AR of Krajina and the order of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Bosanski Novi on the criteria for voluntary resettlement, 5.680 persons with proper documents ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I think we're turning to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "... left the municipality of Bosanski Novi on 23 July 1992 and emigrated with the assistance of UNPROFOR and the High Commission for Refugees to Croatia, Slovenia, and other countries of western Europe." So, here, the Banja Luka CSB is concluding that the ARK Crisis Staff 's decisions on resettlement were, in fact, implemented in Bosanski Novi; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it wasn't a decision. It was a conclusion. Secondly, I cannot answer that question just like that. This was done only in July. I claim that it was impossible until the breakthrough of the police or perhaps -- corridor or maybe only with the police. And if I'm not mistaken, May, June. And it's the Executive Council of the government that is being invoked here, and that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to turn now --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Ms. Stewart to play a clip which has been uploaded as 65 ter 22682b, and it will be the second of two clips under that number. We'll have to play it twice. It's a portion of a rally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what about the first of the two clips, will you separate it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We'll seek -- the first is solely to place two particular people there. For efficiency, we'll seek to just speak to the Defence about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin, people's deputy. "Radoslav Brdjanin: Brothers and sisters, dear people of Krajina, and all other patriots who have come to this meeting, we must not succumb to the greatest deceit, that we are voting for war or peace. We are voting for the betrayal or rescues of Republika Srpska. Those leftist forces which are offering us co-existence again must know that it is the obligation of Serbs over the next hundred years to wipe their feet from the foul non-Christians who have befouled this land of ours. Also it is not true that we do not know where our borders lie. Our borders extend from Benkovac to Trebinje, our borders extend from the Hungarian border all the way to Sokolac, and I hope with the capital of Belgrade when we say that we are a national Serbian state ... we must tell the world that on Serbian land no one has the right to proclaim those were defeated as victors because this is the native land of Tsar Dusan, Prince Lazar, Karadjordje, and the Serbian heros of today. I urge you to participate in the referendum in large numbers, because that referendum, let me warn you, offers to us that we cede 20 populated places of which 13 are cities. It offers to us that we return to Alija and Tudjman and live with them. And I suggest that we put up a barbed wire and say that never gain will our enemies spread throughout Krajina and attack us for the fifth or fourth time in this century. The worst thing is that some individuals have now remembered that war should not have been waged, as we were the ones who imposed war. Some have now remembered that NATO is dangerous. Do those gentlemen know that our lives, the lives of those of us who are married and have children are several times cheaper than the lives of the young men lying in their graves on their behalf? Dammed be the one who betrays Republika Srpska and the interests of the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I can just draw your attention to one translation issue, I guess. It's on page 52, line 21. It was referred here in the translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is anything which is relevant at this moment, then we would deal with it. If --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe it can create a confusion. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd ask that if the witness doesn't speak English, he be asked to remove his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you speak English, Mr. Sajic? Mr. Sajic, do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You responded to my question when you had your earphones off. Do you understand any English? Do you understand any English or no English at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is nothing major. Only here it was referred to "Krajina." And it should be "Krajina square." So that's the only issue I have with this translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's 52, line 21. It says: "Spread throughout Krajina." And on B/C/S, Brdjanin said: "Through Krajina square."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that being a square --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In Banja Luka. That's your -- okay. Then I take it that that will not be the focus of your questions, Mr. Traldi. But it will be verified. Could I, while we are in -- I also saw a -- in the beginning I saw the text with the name of the speaker, Mr. Brdjanin, and then what his position was, and halfway there was another text on the screen which I had no time to read much but it's looked as direct --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... direct stream.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Direct stream, yes. I -- when I had deciphered "direct" then I didn't know what the rest was, which means that it was broadcasted directly or at least?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what it says on this recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's my understanding, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, in the last image here, we see the top of the banner on the right. What we see is "cvi srbi," or "all Serbs," and what would be below that if we could see it would read "in one state"; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to see it I could say yes, but what I see now is all Serbs, "cvi srbi."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin says here at the beginning of the video: "It is the obligation of Serbs over the next 100 years to wipe their feet from the foul non-Christians who have befouled this soil of ours." This is one of the derogatory public speeches that Mr. Brdjanin made that we discussed earlier in your testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when this speech was made. That I did not see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. It was not when but whether this is a derogatory speech of the kind Mr. Brdjanin made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood the contents of the speech as saying that we need to come to our senses. I don't even know what the vote was about, so I cannot comment on it. Why the referendum?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please focus on the line that was brought to your attention: "It's the obligation of Serbs over the next 100 years to wipe their feet from the foul non-Christians who have befouled this soil of ours." That is what Mr. Traldi was drawing your attention to when he asked you whether this was a derogatory public speech as Mr. Brdjanin made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see. From the context he's not denying. He's just saying if you don't win, you will be cleaning the shoes of those who did such and such a thing in World War II to us. I mean, it's a bit nationalist. These are meetings, rallies that were held frequently in our part of the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to test your evidence a little bit on that. When he refers to foul non-Christians. Calling them "foul," that's derogatory; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For us it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And when he suggests that their presence has befouled the soil of Republika Srpska. That's derogatory too; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are authorities that he is talking about, not the people. Somebody wins power, and then you have Sarajevo, Izetbegovic, and so on. He meant the authorities, those in power, not the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He says the foul non-Christians, not the foul SDA members, the foul HDZ members, the foul members of the Patriotic League. He says the foul non-Christians. That means everybody; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when the speech was given. It would be easier for me if I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Our records indicate 1994.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are still war time speeches. It wasn't just one sentence that he spoke. It's a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In another sentence in the speech, he suggests that the Serbs "put up a barbed wire and say that never again will our enemies spread." Putting up a barbed wire means keeping out the people who had left the area; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We're not putting up the barbed wire. He's referring to barbed wire as some sort of something. You could just understand it as a concept, as a comparison. I mean, where would you put up barbed wire in the Krajina square? I mean, this was in the centre of Banja Luka. You cannot put barbed wire up in the Krajina square in the centre of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Right. It's a concept a comparison, a metaphor?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Metaphor, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Barbed wire, he is using it as a metaphor because barbed wire is something that you use to keep people out; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends. I mean, somebody uses electricity, barbed wire is a concept involving Jasenovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we get interpretation Jasenovac, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is not a matter of interpretation but rather a reference to a historical event. Could you clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, when you say Jasenovac, you're referring to a camp where Serbs were held, many killed, during the Second World War; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And barbed wire at that camp would have been used to restrict people's movement; right? In that case, to stop them from going out.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that the mention of barbed wire would make us to remember Jasenovac. I'm not saying that that was that comparison. I mean, the same thing would happen if you mentioned the river Sava, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, let's try to keep matters a bit shorter. The reference to barbed wire and enemies never spread again, is that a reference to enemies not to return where Serbs are living at that moment? In your understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have listened to this footage twice. It's the first time and the second time he is referring to the Krajina square and barbed wire, and he probably is referring to that kind of rule never returning to Banja Luka again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What rule do you mean? My question was simple, not for you to explain what you heard but whether the reference to the barbed wire and the enemies never spread again, and I on purpose left out where, not exactly, whether that's a reference to enemies that should not return where Serbs are living. Is that your understanding of it or is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that this was the Krajina square that they were talking about and that it should not return there. As for the rest, I'm not quite sure I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- you said it was a metaphor. Are you really telling us that you believe that it was all to keep the enemies out of that specific square, wherever they could -- they could move in the streets around, they could move in the villages, they could move in everywhere apart from that square? Is that your understanding? Then please tell us so that we can ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He mentioned the Krajina square. It's not clear to me what he was actually saying in that speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, the Chamber would not mind if you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I would ask that the video before marked for identification before I do. We'll speak with the Defence about the first clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Madam Registrar still would like to have the CD, I take it. Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22682b receives number P6976, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have to P2875.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This document comes from the 1st Krajina Corps command. It's dated the 1st of June, 1992. Directing your attention to the end of the third paragraph, we read: "A portion of the Muslim and Croatian population, is moving out and the region of Bosnian Krajina has issued a decision to facilitate such departures providing that the Serbs from Central Bosnia and places with predominantly Muslim and Croatian populations were also allowed to move out. Those departing will not be allowed to return." Now this is describing the conclusions that we just saw from the 29th of May ARK Crisis Staff meeting that we looked at last session; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the description that those departing will not be allowed to return, that's consistent with Mr. Brdjanin's speech about not letting enemies come back; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. You're linking the speech and this document here, and they have nothing to do with each other. Vukic was writing about this, and nobody was moving out. Brdja was speaking in 1994, whereas the document talks about 1992. In my opinion, these two things are not related at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, first you say nobody was moving out. The document reports, in fact, that a portion of the Muslim and Croatian population is moving out. That's true what Colonel Vukelic has written there, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true. It wasn't so. Vukelic was Talic's assistant for morale and he was submitting a report, information, in which he was saying that people were moving out, but he didn't know it. Nobody could move out. You can see that this was the 1st of June and on the 28th the corridor was broken through. I mean, it's just information. The document needs to be reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's clear from this that the information that the 1st Krajina Corps had was that people were moving out; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's writing this information but it's not actually there. He is writing it, sending it to his commander, and they both live in Banja Luka and they're aware that there is no mass departure. The 1st of June, this is the time that I'm speaking about, and it's quite another thing what Brdja was talking about in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's focus on the last sentence: "Those departing will not be allowed to return." The rationale behind that was to allow Serbs to move in; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Let me hear it again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The rationale behind not allowing those Muslims and Croats to return was to allow Serbs to move into their places; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that. I know of the following: Serbs were not allowed to come back as deserters. I don't know that this had to do with Muslims. I don't see that anywhere here. Serbs who were leaving who did not want to defend their hearths, that's what it was referring. Some other people were being killed in their stead. As for Muslims and Croats, I don't know that that refers to them in this document. Perhaps there was some talk about that, but that is not what this document is about. I deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, again, you haven't answered the question I asked you. But let's cut this short.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 31672, page 25, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This will be another portion of your Brdjanin testimony. I'm going to start with what you're asked at the bottom of the page at line 22. You were asked: "In the sense that Bosnian Muslims and Croats who leave will not be allowed to return, period, and you're saying the rational behind that is to allow Serbs to move in; right?" And you respond: "It is linked up in the text. In the statements, it is all linked up. Yes." Do you stand behind this portion of your Brdjanin testimony as truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it has to do with accommodating the Serbs who were thrown out from Slavonia and other areas. As for the corridor and this information, that has nothing to do with that. And I must emphasise, this information was not given to me like this in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, we are at this moment listening for a long time now already to the interpretation of this witness of all kind of documents, and it seems that his interpretation is different from what the -- what the Prosecution is seeking to establish. The Chamber finally will evaluate the entirety of the evidence and it's clear that the witness interprets these materials differently from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I do have one more question and it's on the previous page, but what I've been seeking to establish with this excerpt is that the witness is interpreting this document differently than he has done before in the sworn testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have seen that more than once today as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And could we have page 25 of this document back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we talked earlier about one of the strategic goals of the Bosnian Serbs being not to be in the same state as Muslims and Croats. You were asked about the relationship between these decisions and that strategic goal here. Judge Agius asked you: "The question is doesn't it make sense that the decision in Bosnian Krajina that Muslims and Croats who leave are not going to be allowed to return because strategic goal number 1 is not to be in the same state as Muslims and Croats? That's the question. "In other words, you are being asked to confirm that the decision of the ARK Crisis Staff that those who leave will not be allowed to return fits in the first strategic point mentioned or outlined by Krajisnik according to that report." And you answered: "To leave room from those who will be coming from elsewhere, the Serbs coming from other parts. In that sense, yes." Do you stand today behind your testimony in the Brdjanin case under oath that the ARK Crisis Staff's decision, that Muslims and Croats who left the ARK would not be allowed to return, was part of the first strategic goal set out at the 16th Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by the statement I gave in the Brdjo case, I'm leaving that possibility open, and I'm not saying something else today. As for the strategic goals of cleansing the territory and changing borders so that they would include ethnic holes is not my interpretation of it. I'm not changing my statement, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd put to you that in that case you said in that sense, yes, this did fit in first strategic point. Today you're saying, I'm leaving the possibility open but ... and then a long list of other things. I'd put to you that you are, in fact, changing your testimony about this. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly about this formulation that you put to me, the strategic goals. I understood it differently, so I am having problems about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, could you please repeat the last part of your sentence.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I stand by the statement that I gave. I don't see any difference there. We're just interpreting it differently, the Prosecutor and myself. I don't see that one of the goals was ethnic cleansing, but, rather, the strategic goal of ethnic communities. And as for Muslims and Croats who were moving out and leaving some areas free, it's logical that those areas would be filled by those Serbs arriving from Slavonia and other places. You couldn't leave them empty. They moved into Serb areas over there and then in turn the Serbs moved into theirs, and that would be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Stojanovic, any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sajic, I know you're tired. If you permit me, I will just put a couple of questions to. I will try to be as direct and as brief as possible. Do you remember when you were asked about the conversation between Karadzic and Cizmovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Do you know what post was occupied by the person who participated in that conversation as indicated? His name was Jovan Cizmovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovan Cizmovic, from a well-known family of attorneys, at the time was some judge or something, an attorney. In any case, he was in the legal business. I don't know that he ever held any political or executive position in the area of Banja Luka. He did not perform any such duty. Perhaps he was in the SDS. Let's put it that way. Some sort of commissioner of a republican board or below Karadzic. But in any event, he did not have any official post. This is as far as Cizmovic is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know if that man at any point in time in 1992 was a member of the Banja Luka Municipality Crisis Staff or the ARK Krajina Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. During that period, he was not in either body. He communicated with Pale, actually, but in the town he was not a significant figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know -- actually, I don't want it to be a leading question so I will put the question to you in the following way. At any point in time, were there any party Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were party Crisis Staffs. As far as I know, yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each of the parties. Each of the three parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And touching upon questions that had to do with people who worked with you in the TO, and you mentioned their names as people who were non-Serbs but still remained at their posts. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber how after the 15th of June the TO changed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence in a broader area, but I will speak about Banja Luka because I was in charge there, before the 15th of June was made up of a series of units ranging from squads to companies, and then the Territorial Defence was supposed to restructure its units according to some structure into four light infantry brigades, and these brigades were then -- came under the command of the Krajina Corps. And there was a special staff that was in charge of those brigades. So each municipality formed a light brigade. People who worked in the TO Staffs stayed in each of these brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now to tell us about the people whose names you mentioned, these three colleagues of yours who were not of Serb ethnicity. After the 22nd June 1992, these people remained at their posts?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Some of them stayed at these posts until the end of the war even, and they live in Banja Luka to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to finish with one more topic. At any point in time at meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff, was the -- there any discussion of attempts to prevent the forcible transfer of population from the Krajina area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The ARK Krajina Crisis Staff, did it ever discuss possible attempts to prevent the population from moving out under pressure.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that forcible moving out was prohibited. I know that. It was discussed, and I don't think that anything like that occurred while I was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at D423.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a conclusion that you had the opportunity to see in your cross-examination. We're going to be looking at page 3.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just wait, Mr. Sajic, so you can have some context so that you can see that it's a document that you already looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the following page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You already commented this document. Could you please now look at paragraph 2 of these conclusions, which states: "The Crisis Staff has decided to resolutely oppose all attempts to move the population out by force or any other form of pressure and to prevent any such attempts with all means available under the law." Is this conclusion what you have just told us about as something that was discussed at the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, thank you very much. The Defence of General Mladic has no further questions for you. Thank you very much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. No further questions from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us -- I have one further question. You told about Zoran Kolak. Could you give us the details of what happened to him? What functions he was doing; where he's living now?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Kolak was a member of my Territorial Defence Staff. It was -- he was in charge of security of buildings. That is a very important job because that was security for public facilities, bridges, et cetera. He is a Croat, an ethnic Croat, and he has two children, and his family was a well-known family, Kolak from the Second World War, the partisans, and he remained on the Territorial Defence staff throughout while I was there, that is. I think that he stayed and then he went to the 1st Light Brigade, I think. And after that I think he left Banja Luka and I don't really know where he is right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you told us several times that what you think. You said he stayed with you until you left, that is, the 15th of June?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said he then went to the light infantry brigade you think. Do you know that for sure? You know that for certain?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know -- yes, please. Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember but I know that right now he is not in Banja Luka. But when he comes, he calls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you say he is not in Banja -- you do not know for sure whether he went to this light infantry brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I think he did. I think he belonged to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you don't remember. You do remember now that he is not living in Banja Luka any further. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see him. He's not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So in effect you are telling us you don't know for sure, you don't even remember when he went to the light infantry brigade, and you do not know for sure whether he stayed because you don't see him in Banja Luka, so therefore he may not be in Banja Luka any further. That's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a second. Zdenko Uvalic, a Croat, went to the 2nd Light Brigade and Kolak went to the 1st Light Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So now you do remember. He went to the 1st Light Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went but I don't know how he -- how long he stayed. That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you don't -- actually, you don't know actually what happened with them, at least with Mr. Kolak.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Uvalic, but I know that Kolak lives abroad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm asking you about Kolak and you tell me that you have no firm knowledge about what happened to him and that he is now living abroad.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions. Then, Mr. Sajic, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench. You're excused and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I establish that you did not do anything with the incorrect or the different formulations in the adjudicated facts, so apparently no -- until now, no adequate measures are taken in this respect. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness once we have taken a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break and we'll resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, not yet. I'd first like to use the opportunity to briefly deliver a statement by the Chamber. It is the Chamber will briefly address the Defence submissions on the Chamber's time management guidance. It takes us back to the 25th of August of this year when the Defence made several submissions essentially objecting to the time management guidance delivered by the Chamber on 24th of July. After having carefully reviewing the submissions, it appears to the Chamber that the Defence has misunderstood the guidance offered and finds the Defence submissions in this respect to be without merit. Although the Chamber considers this to be very unfortunate, it sees no value in repeating or attempting to further clarify that which it has already made abundantly clear time and time again. In this respect, the Chamber encourages the Defence to revisit and carefully consider the Chamber's guidance as well as the full record of these proceedings before it jumps to any conclusions that the Chamber is somehow changing the rules concerning the production of evidence. Madam Registrar, you can already go and find the witness. Lastly -- yes, the usher. Yes. Lastly, the Chamber finds the Defence submissions concerning the investigation of witnesses and members of the Defence team difficult to understand. Accordingly, should the Defence intend to pursue these matters, it is instructed to file a motion clearly describing the relevant issues and explicitly stating the relief sought. And this concludes the Chamber's submissions on this matter. We're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, I see it's you who will examine the witness, the witness being Mr. Krsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krsic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I invite to you make the solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Krsic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll find him to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Krsic.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will pause a bit after your answers so that the interpreters could finish interpreting. It's not that I'm not satisfied with your answers. I just need to wait for the interpretation. Could you please just state your name and surname for the record.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: I am Vojislav Krsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, did you want to say something? No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your microphone is on so I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's usually Judge Fluegge reminds me that I should switch it off. But you are taking over his task, I hear. Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm very grateful, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have to take some of your chores, since you are taking many of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krsic, have you provided a statement to the members of General Mladic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have 1D1684 on our screens, please. And with the assistance of the usher, I would like to provide this witness with the witness statement as well and -- first to be shown to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krsic, you now have a hard copy, but you can also see a document on the screen. Can you recognise the signature on the first page of this document?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see the last page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the last page, can you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me not ask you page by page. What is contained on every page, at the bottom of every page?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: Yes, on every page you can see my signature, my original signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsic, what is recorded in this statement, has it been recorded correctly in relation to what you had said to the members of General Mladic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: Yes. This statement records what I said to the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is written in this statement, is it truthful and correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: What is written in this statement is truthful and correct, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsic, if I were to put the same questions to you today, would you give us basically the same answers?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would provide the same answers basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think we were provided with a information note with --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- at least two corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's actually -- yeah. Paragraph 4, you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are returning a favour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we have paragraph 4 on our screens, please. It's on page 2. Although I put it in front of me, I forgot to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krsic --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- you drew my attention to something; namely, that in paragraph 4, you omitted to mention one of the platoons. Do you remember which platoon that would be, the one that you omitted to mention?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I forgot to mention yet another platoon that was within our brigade. That is the independent anti-sabotage platoon, and it also has an abbreviation in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. So in the battalion, there were how many companies and how many platoons when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: I'd like to correct you here. It's not battalions. It is the light infantry brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: In the light infantry brigade, there were seven companies and there were these independent platoons, the ones that are mentioned here plus the one that I referred to just now. That is what I found there when I arrived in the brigade. Later on we established yet another platoon, but that is sometime in October. Actually, this was the reserve of the brigade and we usually called it the intervention platoon. What is referred to here in the statement is the situation that I found there when I arrived to join the light infantry brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now with your assistance and with the assistance of Judge Fluegge, after this correction I have to ask you yet again whether this statement is truthful and correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we would move to offer this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1684 receives number D844, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D844 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I asked for extra time for leading this witness and I -- it's less than hour. It's 55 minutes I asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's a little bit more than the usual 30 minutes. You know that there's a balance for the whole of the presentation of the Defence case, but there's no objection against -- did you say 45 or 55?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fifty five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fifty five, yes. The Chamber, as always, will closely monitor how you use your time but does not object against using more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would -- thank you, Your Honour. I would first read statement summary of Mr. Krsic and then I would pose my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Vojislav Krsic was a professional soldier at the Zagreb garrison until 15th of September, 1991, when he left the JNA with the rank of captain. He came to Kotor Varos in July 1992. And on 28th of August, 1992, he joined the 1st Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade. He was engaged as the assistant to the Chief of Staff for operations and instruction matters. He will speak about the composition of the brigade. Vojislav Krsic will testify about Grabovica, where he was present in person about the beginning of the incident and the persons present there, about the accommodation of Muslim men, soldiers, women, and children at the elementary school building in Grabovica, about the gathering of inhabitants of Grabovica, mainly women in mourning attire. He will speak about the security at the school on the first evening and the stay of the Muslims there, including the tasks he personally issued to the security. He witnessed the arrival of buses, the boarding of women and children, and their departure from Grabovica. He will provide details about the beginning of the incident, the first murder of a Muslim, in which no military personnel were involved. He will also testify that the then-commander of the brigade sent him to the brigade command post at Kotor Varos, and subsequently he was given other tasks, whereby he was moved away from Grabovica and from further developments in the village. Vojislav Krsic will also testify that not a single shell that had been fired under his command was directed against civilian targets. He will testify that it was never said that the area in which his unit was located should be ethnically cleansed, let alone attempted to implement such a thing in practice. And Mr. Krsic testifies that his brigade was of multi-ethnic composition. That would be statement summary and now I have several questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can have paragraph 6 of Mr. Krsic's statement. It's on the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krsic, you do see a paragraph 6 before you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first sentence in this paragraph says: "At the time I joined the brigade, it was completely disorganised." I'd like to ask you something in relation to this. This statement refers to which period? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: This statement refers to the period from the very establishment of the brigade until, say, November. It could be put that way. However, we made significant efforts in that direction, say, in the month of October and November.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us now why you believe that the brigade was disorganised.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: As regards military units, the word "organisational establishment structure" is used. So it is this concept that is used in all armies in the world, including our army. So the first word, "structure," means that it has its command, its staff units, its combat units, logistics units or unit, and so on. The second part of this composite phrase, "establishment," means that there is something to be said for each and every one of these elements. As regards specialty, as regards type of military weapons and so on. So that unit, as a whole, is able to function on that basis. When I arrived in the Kotor Varos Brigade, that requirement, as far as organisational establishment structure is concerned, had not been met. First of all, that brigade did not have a developed command of its own. That ask one element. Secondly, the units that were organisational elements of that brigade, from an organisational establishment point of view, did not have the necessary personnel. I'm just going to mention something by way of illustration, say, the pioneer platoon that was one of the elements of the organisational establishment structure. The pioneer platoon is an engineering unit or, rather, a unit that is supposed to be manned by persons who have engineering as their VES. However, the 35 men we had on that platoon included only five persons that met that requirement. Thirty men did not have that military speciality at all; engineering, that is. So that is what I would have to say about the organisational establishment structure, namely, that this brigade was not organised according to these rules as otherwise required by the former JNA and military rules in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've already mentioned to us the intervention platoon that was established later. Why is it important and what was it that wasn't organised there before it had been established, that is?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in the brigade, there was no reserve in this brigade. Otherwise, a basic rule as far as combat disposition and combat readiness of units of is concerned, everyone should have a reserve. If there's a crisis possibly in some part of the combat disposition, then that reserve can be used, or rather in that way such a weakness can be eliminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another segment of this same question: The command of the 1st Krajina Corps, what was its attitude towards the 1st Kotor Varos Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: As far as the Kotor Varos Brigade is concerned, the following facts should be pointed out: The Kotor Varos Brigade was one of the most recent units established in the 1st Krajina Corps. That is one fact. Another important fact is something I've already mentioned; that is to say, organisationally or logistically it was not provided for, and that was necessary in order to have it carry out its tasks properly and fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Who was appointed commander and how did the command function of the 1st Kotor Varos Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: With the order of the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, I don't remember the date but I think that was the 11th of June, 1992. The Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade was to be formed, and the order specified that Slobodan Zupljanin should be the commander of the brigade. However, Slobodan Zupljanin was never in the Kotor Varos Brigade and he was never actually the commander of that brigade. In the initial period the brigade did not even have a commander. I came to Kotor Varos sometime on the 22nd of July, and from the 22nd of July until early August sometime, I contacted the Kotor Varos Brigade command, and only Mane Tepic was there with a couple of officers, but he was not in the commander in the true sense of having been appointed to that duty. He was just co-ordinating all the tasks and carrying out the co-ordination among the two units in the field. The brigade at the time did not have its commander. It was only later in agreement with the Kotor Varos War Presidency and the 22nd Infantry Brigade and probably in consultation with the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, the commander of the brigade was Dusan Novakovic, lieutenant-colonel. When I came to the brigade on the 22nd of August, I had a meeting. I met commander, Dusan Novakovic there. He received me and he assigned me to the post of assistance chief for operations and training. As for the relationship between the Kotor Varos Brigade and the 1st Krajina Corps command - in fact, the Kotor Varos Brigade in that sense was like an orphan because during that period it was not actually in the system and in the command and control system by the corps command, particularly not from the logistical aspect. The Kotor Varos Brigade logistics, for the most part, was entrusted to the Kotor Varos municipality and the Presidency. So the actual relationship between the 1st Krajina Corps and the light infantry brigade actually began in late November or December 1992 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now about the communications system in the Kotor Varos Brigade and what was the communications system with the 1st Krajina Corps command, let's say, from the time you arrived until December.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: As far as the communications system is concerned, first of all I have to say that within the brigade we had considerable problems. The combat disposition of the units of the Kotor Varos Brigade was quite spread out. They were located in local communes which were quite far from the command post, which was located in Kotor Varos. So in this initial period, the brigade only had a few older devices, RUK1, RUK1B, which were practically outdated, especially in former JNA units. So we didn't have very strong links between the command and the subordinate units. This is one side of this whole issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which command and which subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: Between the command of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade and its organisational units; i.e., the light infantry companies which were deployed predominantly in the areas of the local communes. And for the second part of the question that has to do with the relationship or the communications between the light infantry brigade command and the corps command: Until November we practically didn't have a proper link between the two commands. It was only later when I became the Chief of Staff I put in a lot of effort to set up proper communications so then later we had both land-lines and telegraph communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us briefly how did you manage the problem of the shortage of communication means.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about the problem of communications and the way we resolved it, we didn't receive the devices from the logistics base, which was quite normal, from the 1st Krajina Corps command. We used some other private channels to obtain these devices from the 2nd Krajina Corps. That was when we received more modern devices, RUP12 for example, which was a standard communications device in the JNA at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: This was already when our logistics needs and communications with the 2nd Krajina Corps started in October and then it went on after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did you receive orders and did you send combat reports to the command of the 1 Krajina Corps and did you receive anything back from them?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC
utterances.text: As for the first part, I am speaking about the point in time when I became the Chief of Staff of the brigade, we did not receive orders directly from the 1st Krajina Corps command. The orders that we received usually came via the command of the 22nd Infantry Brigade. I assume that one of the reasons for that was due to the communications system, such as it was, and the way I have already described. So for the most part, the light infantry brigade did not always send reports directly to the 1st Krajina Corps command, combat reports or new other types of reports. Sometimes we would send it through the command of the 22nd Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm looking at the clock. Mr. Krsic, we'll adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30. But before you leave this courtroom, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way, with whomever, about your testimony, whether that's testimony given today or it's testimony still to be given tomorrow. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 4th of December, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of December, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.
